prompt: In `regression_losses.py`, MSE's best single guess for the seven deliveries is 20.57 minutes. What is that number?
hint: Compare it with the line printed under the three guesses.

choices.text: The median of the seven times
choices.why: The median is 14.0, and it is what MAE chose.

choices.text: Their mean
choices.why: Right. The constant with the lowest squared error is the mean, and one storm dragged it to a time nobody waited.

choices.text: The time of the most common delivery
choices.why: That is 14, which appears twice; MSE's answer is far from it.

choices.text: The midpoint between the fastest delivery and the slowest
choices.why: That would be 36 minutes, halfway from 12 to 60.

prompt: At a guess of 15, the storm delivery pulls with -90 under MSE and with -2 under Huber. Why only -2 under Huber?
hint: What does `np.clip` do to the error?

choices.text: Huber ignores any point whose error is above its threshold
choices.why: It does not ignore it: the storm still pulls, with -2, as hard as an ordinary delivery 2 minutes off.

choices.text: Huber divides each error by the mean error of the set
choices.why: No mean appears in its definition; the slope is the error, capped.

choices.text: Past `DELTA` its slope stops growing and stays at 2
choices.why: Right. Huber is a straight line beyond the threshold, so a huge error pulls no harder than one of exactly 2.

choices.text: Huber squares the error and halves it
choices.why: That is its shape below the threshold, where the storm is not.

prompt: Suppose an eighth delivery took 25 minutes. Under MSE, with what pull would it act on a guess of 15? Use the program's formula, `2 * (15 - minutes)`.
hint: The error is the guess minus the delivery.

prompt: Which of the four cases in `xent.py` has the highest cross-entropy loss?
hint: The loss looks at one probability.

choices.text: Unsure, wrong
choices.why: It costs 1.386: the right class still had 0.25.

choices.text: Unsure, with the right class barely ahead
choices.why: It costs 0.886, less than either wrong case.

choices.text: Confident and wrong
choices.why: Right: 4.036, because the right class got 0.018 and minus its log is large.

choices.text: Confident and right, because its gradient is the largest
choices.why: Its loss is 0.036 and its gradient on the right class is the smallest, -0.035.

prompt: With softmax and cross-entropy, what is the gradient of the loss with respect to the logit of the right class?
hint: Look at the first number of each gradient in the output, next to `p`.

choices.text: Its probability minus 1
choices.why: Right: -0.982 when it had 0.018, -0.035 when it had 0.965. The push grows with the mistake.

choices.text: Minus the log of its probability
choices.why: That is the loss itself, not its slope.

choices.text: Zero, since the loss already includes that class
choices.why: It is the largest gradient in the row whenever the network is wrong.

choices.text: One over its probability
choices.why: That is the slope of the log with respect to p; the softmax's slope cancels most of it, leaving p - 1.

prompt: A network that gives each of ten classes 0.1 has a cross-entropy of 2.303. What is the loss of an untrained network that gives each of 100 classes the same probability? Three decimal places.
hint: Minus the natural log of the right class's probability.

prompt: Why may `tinynet.softmax_cross_entropy` subtract the largest logit from every logit without changing the probabilities?
hint: Write the fraction with the shift in it.

choices.text: Because the loss depends on the largest logit alone
choices.why: The loss reads the right class's logit, which is not the largest when the network is wrong.

choices.text: A factor `exp(-m)` appears above and below the fraction, and cancels
choices.why: Right. Softmax depends on the differences between logits, and a common shift leaves those untouched.

choices.text: It changes them a little, but by too little to show in four decimal places
choices.why: The change is exactly zero in exact arithmetic; `0.1270` was printed by both versions.

choices.text: Because `float32` rounds all large numbers to the same value
choices.why: Large values overflow to infinity rather than rounding together, which is why the shift is needed.

prompt: During training, one batch holds an image the network gets wrong by 120 in its logits, and tinynet reports the batch's loss as `inf`. What happens to the weights at that step?
hint: Which of tinynet's two return values does the update use?

choices.text: They all become `nan`, and training is lost
choices.why: That is what a `nan` gradient does; tinynet's gradient for that image was `[-1, 1, 0]`, finite.

choices.text: They move normally, since the gradient `p - target` stays finite
choices.why: Right. Only the reported loss is broken; the step corrects the mistake as usual.

choices.text: They stay as they were, because an infinite loss skips the step
choices.why: Nothing in the loop looks at the loss before stepping.

choices.text: They move by an infinite amount and overflow
choices.why: The step is the gradient times the rate, and the gradient is between -1 and 1.

prompt: PyTorch's cross-entropy takes the network's raw ___ and does the log-sum-exp itself, so a softmax applied beforehand is a bug.
hint: The scores the last layer produces, one per class.

prompt: `multilabel.py` gives an 8 the probabilities 0.957, 0.979 and 0.76, which add up to 2.697. What does that sum mean?
hint: What ties the three outputs together?

choices.text: The network is overconfident and needs a softmax at the end
choices.why: A softmax would force the three to share 1, and an 8 really is even, above 4 and looped.

choices.text: The loss is computed wrongly, since probabilities add up to 1
choices.why: Probabilities of one choice among several add up to 1; these are three separate questions.

choices.text: Nothing: each output is a separate yes-or-no probability
choices.why: Right. Three independent sigmoids, three independent answers, and their total is not a quantity.

choices.text: The image is expected to belong to about three classes
choices.why: It answers three questions, and that it got three yeses is the content, not the sum.

prompt: A yes-or-no output gives `p = 0.9` to an image whose answer is no. Which expression is its binary cross-entropy?

choices.why: That is the loss when the answer is yes.
Right: the probability the output gave to no is 0.1, and the loss is minus its log, about 2.3.
That is a squared error on the probability, which is not this loss.
Only one of the two terms applies to a given answer; the target picks it.

prompt: A model tags recipes with any of 40 labels, such as vegetarian, spicy and quick. Which last layer and loss fit?
hint: Can a recipe be spicy and quick at once?

choices.text: 40 logits, a softmax, and cross-entropy
choices.why: Softmax makes the labels compete for one share of 1, so a spicy quick vegetarian dish would be forced to pick one.

choices.text: 40 logits, and binary cross-entropy on each
choices.why: Right: one independent yes-or-no question per label, as `multilabel.py` did with three.

choices.text: One logit, and MSE against the number of labels
choices.why: A count says how many labels and loses which ones.

choices.text: 40 linear outputs with MSE against the 0-or-1 targets
choices.why: It trains, slowly and with outputs that are not probabilities; a sigmoid with binary cross-entropy is the fitting pair.

prompt: On the confidently wrong image, MSE's gradient on the right class is -0.0013 against cross-entropy's -0.9997. Why is MSE's so small?
hint: What does a softmax with one class near 1 do under a small change of a logit?

choices.text: MSE's loss for that image is small, and a small loss has a small slope
choices.why: It is 1.993, at MSE's ceiling of 2; the loss is large and its slope is not.

choices.text: A saturated softmax is nearly flat, and MSE must pass through it
choices.why: Right. Cross-entropy's log cancels that flat slope; MSE has nothing to cancel it.

choices.text: The learning rate of 0.1 is too low for MSE
choices.why: The gradient was computed on one image with no learning rate involved.

choices.text: MSE squares the gradient on its way back through the network
choices.why: It squares the error; its gradient on p is 2(p - target), which here is large.

prompt: Someone repeats the race but gives the MSE run a different seed. MSE's run then ends 0.003 above cross-entropy's. What can be concluded?
hint: What else changed besides the loss?

choices.text: MSE is the better loss for the digits after all
choices.why: Two things changed at once, so the result cannot be credited to either.

choices.text: Cross-entropy wins with seed 0 and loses with the others
choices.why: One run with another seed says little about the rest.

choices.text: The final epoch is where the losses are compared, so MSE wins
choices.why: And the gap of 0.003 sits inside what a different start alone produces.

choices.text: Little: the starting weights and batch order differ too, so the race is no longer fair
choices.why: Right. A fair comparison changes one thing; lesson 18 measures how far seeds alone move a result.

hint: What question does the output answer?

Recognising which digit an image shows
pairs.right: Cross-entropy on one logit per class

prompt: In `metric.py`, model C has the lowest cross-entropy and the lowest accuracy. How does that happen?
hint: Look at how wrong C is when it is wrong.

choices.text: Cross-entropy rewards a model for being wrong
choices.why: It charges every wrong answer; C's are cheap because each is barely wrong.

choices.text: Each of its mistakes is mild, at 0.45
choices.why: Right. Cross-entropy cares how wrong; accuracy counts how often. B has one answer at 0.001 and pays for it.

choices.text: Accuracy is computed with a threshold of 0.9 instead of 0.5
choices.why: The program uses `p > 0.5`.

choices.text: Five questions are too few for a loss to mean anything
choices.why: The arithmetic is exact at five; the disagreement is real.

prompt: A team wants to train directly on accuracy, since accuracy is what they report. Why does gradient descent fail on it?
hint: Lesson 1 met the same problem in the perceptron's step.

choices.text: Accuracy is too slow to compute on a batch
choices.why: It is a comparison and a mean, cheaper than cross-entropy.

choices.text: Accuracy rises when the loss should fall, so the signs are reversed
choices.why: Flipping a sign would be trivial; the problem is that there is no slope to flip.

choices.text: A small weight change changes no prediction, so its slope is zero
choices.why: Right. With no slope there is no direction to step in; a smooth loss gives one, and accuracy judges the result.

choices.text: Accuracy is undefined on the validation set
choices.why: It is defined anywhere there are labels; the lesson reports it on validation.

prompt: Put the steps of a numerically stable cross-entropy for one image in order.
hint: The shift comes before any exponential.
items: Subtract the largest logit from every logit
Take the exponential of each shifted logit
Add the exponentials and take the log of the sum
Subtract the right class's shifted logit from that log

choices.why: Yes: 20.57 for both.

choices.text: tinynet's loss stayed finite when the network was wrong by 120

choices.text: Cross-entropy was ahead of MSE in validation accuracy at every epoch
choices.why: Yes: from 0.714 against 0.322 after one epoch to 0.953 against 0.944 after twenty.

choices.text: The three multilabel outputs for each digit added up to 1
choices.why: No: 0.0 for the 3 and 2.697 for the 8.

choices.text: Two models with the same accuracy had different cross-entropy
